section_summary: This section details State Department and Navy Department correspondence from 1934 to 1939 monitoring the expansion, strategic capabilities, and movements of Japan's merchant marine and fishing fleet. Comprehensive reports from the American Consulate in Kobe assess the naval auxiliary value of fast motor freighters and tankers constructed under Japan's subsidized Ship Improvement programs, noting defense adaptations such as gun placements and high speeds. Later records trace individual Japanese merchant and fishing vessels operating in foreign waters, including operations off Baja California, Liberia, the Caribbean, and Mexican oil ports.

subfiles.about: Comprehensive voluntary report evaluating the military and naval capabilities of Japan's subsidized merchant fleet.
subfiles.from: Robert Mills McClintock, Vice Consul at Kobe
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul McClintock provides an exhaustive strategic analysis of thirty-one high-speed motor freighters and tankers built under Japan's 1932 Ship Improvement Law. He highlights their 18-knot speed and large cargo capacity, warning they provide the Japanese Navy with superior potential fleet auxiliaries and transports compared to slower American vessels. The study also identifies Japan's strategic vulnerability to petroleum blockades and notes the commercial drive behind transpacific route expansion.
subfiles.title: The Strategical Value of Japan's New Merchant Fleet

subfiles.about: Supplemental report examining Japanese budgetary cuts to shipping subsidies and naval payments for special defense installations.
subfiles.from: Robert Mills McClintock, Vice Consul at Kobe
subfiles.summary: This supplemental report reviews changes in Japan's shipbuilding program following the Finance Ministry's reduction of construction subsidies for fiscal 1935-1936. McClintock reveals that the Imperial Navy secretly paid five yen per ton under the 1932 program for defense installations, including gun placements confirmed aboard Nippon Yusen Kaisha freighters. He assesses high-speed naval tankers operated by Iino Shoji and notes that major lines continue building fast, militarily useful liners.
subfiles.title: Supplement: The Strategical Value of Japan's New Merchant Fleet
